title: Civic participation is becoming an AI-mediated public-service layer, shifting legitimacy toward listening, translation, moderation, and feedback capacity
source_unit: European Commission Reform and Investment Task Force, Improving Civic Participation with Emerging Technologies, published 3 September 2026, with OECD companion analysis
geography: European Union project involving Portugal, Spain, and the Netherlands; ecosystem evidence involving 21 EU member states

lead_countries.unit: participating lead countries: Portugal, Spain, and the Netherlands

ecosystem_actors.unit: more than 600 public-sector, private, civil-society, academic, and innovation-ecosystem actors engaged

member_states.unit: EU member states represented in ecosystem engagement

institutional_route.value: Participation technology is being organized as a public-sector capability and innovation ecosystem, not only as a standalone consultation website

observations.method: European Commission project description and results summary; the publication reports project activities and ecosystem engagement rather than a representative population survey or causal evaluation.
observations.uncertainty: Actor counts describe participation in the project ecosystem, not citizen participation rates, public legitimacy, or successful policy adoption.
observations.subgroup: Public administrations, civic-technology actors, civil society, academia, private-sector innovators, and participating countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large ecosystem engagement can reflect institutional and funding priorities rather than broad public demand; projects may remain pilot-scale.

denominator.unit: three-country project and three prototype cases

prototypes.unit: AI-enabled prototypes: ConsultationAI in the Netherlands, OnRecord in Portugal, and ParticipApp in Spain

bootcamp_participants.unit: more than 90 participants in the February 2025 Lisbon co-creation bootcamp

prototype_functions.value: The prototypes aim to improve citizens' participation experience while expanding government capacity to listen to and analyze needs and contributions

deployment_stage.value: Prototypes were being tested and refined before deployment; Portugal's prototype was described as being embedded in Participa.gov

observations.method: OECD project analysis and European Commission implementation summary; prototypes are described as pilots and development pathways, not completed outcome evaluations.
observations.uncertainty: The sources do not establish adoption scale, user satisfaction, representativeness of input, policy influence, or whether AI improves deliberative quality.
observations.subgroup: Participants in public consultations, public servants, civil-society organizations, designers, researchers, and civic technologists.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI may reduce administrative burden while also creating opaque filtering, translation loss, vendor dependence, or a false appearance of listening.

observations.period: 2025; diagnosed participation bottlenecks and technology opportunities

denominator.unit: OECD policy analysis of case studies, desk research, and stakeholder interviews

trust_barrier.unit: percent of citizens on average across the OECD reported as tending not to trust their governments in the cited evidence

consultation_adoption_doubt.unit: percent OECD average cited as tending not to trust that government would adopt opinions expressed in a public consultation

participation_bottlenecks.value: Feedback and accountability gaps, weak connection to decision-making, exclusion, poor process design, isolation from wider society, undue influence, and limited public-authority capacity are identified as barriers

technology_opportunities.value: AI can analyze large input volumes, moderate large conversations, translate or explain complex material, connect small-group deliberation to broader publics, and support immersive scenario work

observations.method: OECD synthesis drawing on analysis, case studies, and interviews; the cited percentages are cross-national averages from underlying evidence and are not a current causal estimate of the pilots.
observations.uncertainty: Technology opportunities are prospective; the report does not show that AI moderation, synthesis, translation, or immersive tools improve trust, inclusion, or policy outcomes in practice.
observations.subgroup: OECD populations and institutions covered by the underlying participation and trust evidence; no single common respondent sample is asserted for all findings.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same tools can amplify misinformation, unequal access, toxic online environments, privacy threats, and environmental costs; more input processing may not equal more democratic power.

denominator.unit: OECD recommendations and European Commission project guardrails

guardrails.value: Transparency, accountability, contestability, complaint and redress mechanisms, human rights, civic freedoms, open documentation, and public involvement in design and governance are recommended

analogue_alternative.value: Governments are advised to provide in-person or low-tech alternatives and invest in digital and AI skills so emerging technology does not become a participation prerequisite

capacity_dependency.value: AI-enabled participation requires public-sector skills, sustainable funding, interoperability, and safeguards against vendor and data lock-in

legitimacy_test.value: The democratic value of the system depends on whether public input remains traceable, contestable, inclusive, and visibly connected to decisions

observations.method: OECD policy recommendations and European Commission project results; these are governance prescriptions, not measured impacts.
observations.uncertainty: The sources do not establish which safeguards will be adopted, enforced, or sufficient across participating administrations.
observations.subgroup: People with limited digital access or skills, public servants, civic organizations, participants in consultations, and communities exposed to automated filtering or classification.
observations.counterinterpretation: Analog alternatives and human oversight may preserve inclusion but also raise cost and staffing requirements, slowing scale or limiting geographic reach.

related_sources.claim: European Commission project scope, countries, prototype work, ecosystem engagement, and results.
OECD evidence framing participation bottlenecks, technology opportunities, risks, and recommendations.
OECD account of prototypes, AI-mediated participation functions, inclusion, redress, capacity, and interoperability conditions.

boundary: This record adds a civic-participation infrastructure route from AI-mediated listening and input processing through public-sector capacity, inclusion, transparency, contestability, feedback, and democratic legitimacy. It does not establish that the prototypes improve participation, trust, policy quality, representation, or outcomes; reported actor and prototype counts are project outputs, not population-level adoption.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official European Commission and OECD pages reviewed for project scope, actor reach, prototypes, participation bottlenecks, prospective technology functions, risks, and governance safeguards.
